### The Genesis of an Empire: From Plague to Privilege

The silk trade in Lyon began not in celebration but in desperation. In 1536, the city was ravaged by a devastating outbreak of the plague that killed over 5,000 residents. Out of this catastrophe, King Francis I issued an edict offering tax exemptions and privileges to silk workers from Genoa and Calabria who were willing to settle in Lyon and teach their craft. This migration marked the genesis of the industry, but it was under the reign of Catherine de Medici and her son, King Henry II, that the true foundation was laid. In the mid-16th century, a severe shortage of luxury fabrics forced the Crown to incentivize domestic production. Lyon was designated as the center of this effort. The King organized the formation of the "Communauté" of silk workers and instituted strict trade fairs, effectively turning Lyon into a royal monopoly for luxury textile production. This era was defined by the importation of expertise and the establishment of royal protection, transforming a city once known solely for banking and trade into the cradle of French haute couture.

### Why a Paged Cache Wins for Serving

A paged key-value cache outperforms a contiguous one for a serving engine primarily because of its superior memory management. A contiguous cache typically requires large, monolithic blocks of memory to be allocated and freed as the cache size grows and shrinks. This leads to two major problems: **memory fragmentation** and **high-latency operations**. As the engine serves requests, it will naturally evict older items and insert new ones. In a contiguous system, freeing a block of memory might create a "hole" that is too small for the next large item, forcing the system to either reject it or perform expensive, slow compaction operations to create a larger free block. This unpredictability makes it difficult to maintain a stable cache size and can cause request latency to spike unexpectedly.

### The Fundamental Concept: KV Caches and State

To understand prefix-cache eviction, one must first understand how inference engines (like vLLM, TGI, or TensorRT-LLM) manage state. When a Large Language Model processes text, it converts tokens into numerical representations via a **Key-Value (KV) Cache**. This cache stores the intermediate attention states (the "context") of the model. During autoregressive generation, the model looks back at this cache to predict the next token without reprocessing the entire input sequence.

**Prefix Caching** is an optimization strategy that realizes that many queries share common beginnings. For example, every request in a customer support bot might start with the same system prompt: *"You are a helpful assistant..."* Instead of re-computing the KV states for this system prompt for every single user, the engine caches the KV values for that prefix once. Subsequent requests identify that the prefix matches the cache, "jump" to that cached state, and only compute the KV values for the unique, user-specific part of the prompt.
